The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $y$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14243863/assets/e2c83b965f7108bff3165531446cce43006a41b9742914e8fc40c50741230427.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $y=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{5}{16}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{11}{16}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{11}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the positive answer since $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So our final answer is $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{11}}{4}.$
